text: Group memberships don't mean much until they unlock actual access on a file server. In this last lesson of the chapter, we'll cover the five NTFS permission levels, the three share permission levels, how the two combine when someone connects over the network, and a worked example showing exactly what a real user ends up able to do.

NTFS permissions live on the file system itself, set on a folder's Security tab, so they apply whether access is local or over the network. Full Control allows everything, plus changing permissions and taking ownership. Modify adds read, write, execute, and delete. Read & Execute allows viewing and running, with no changes. Read is view-only, and Write allows adding or editing files without necessarily being able to read everyone else's. These apply to whoever sits in that folder's access control list — almost always a security group.

Share permissions are a separate, older layer, set on the Sharing tab instead of Security, that only matters when a folder is accessed over the network through its share — they're skipped entirely for someone logged in locally at the server. They have only three levels: Full Control, Change, and Read. Many administrators leave share permissions wide open and do all the real access control with NTFS instead, but older environments often lock down both layers independently. When both apply, Windows combines each one into its own effective permission, then grants whichever of the two is more restrictive.

Say the share Finance-Employees permission is Change, but the NTFS permission for that same group is Read & Execute. Jordan Lee, a member of that group, connects over the network. Change would allow writing and deleting; Read & Execute doesn't. Since the more restrictive one wins, Jordan's actual effective access is Read & Execute — he can open and run files, but can't save changes or delete anything.

That's NTFS and share permissions, and how most restrictive wins when the two disagree — it closes out identity, groups, and access in this chapter. Next, in Chapter 2, we'll cover Group Policy Objects and how they actually apply across that OU tree you built in Lesson 2.
